title: Inheritance
description: Explore class hierarchies through inheritance, including base/derived classes, abstract classes, virtual methods, and the sealed modifier.

data.text: Inheritance is one of the four pillars of OOP. It allows a class (the derived or child class) to inherit fields, properties, and methods from another class (the base or parent class). This promotes code reuse and establishes an 'is-a' relationship: a Dog is an Animal, a Car is a Vehicle.

Inheritance models a natural hierarchical relationship. If you can truthfully say 'X is a Y', then X can likely inherit from Y. A Manager is an Employee. A CheckingAccount is a BankAccount. This relationship flows in one direction: a Manager inherits from Employee, but Employee does not inherit from Manager.

data.caption: A typical class inheritance hierarchy in an e-commerce application

data.text: The base class (also called parent or superclass) contains the members that derived classes inherit. The derived class (also called child or subclass) adds or overrides behavior. In C#, you specify the base class using a colon after the class name: `public class Dog : Animal`.

data.title: Base and Derived Classes
data.content: An Animal base class with a Dog and Cat derived class that override the Speak behavior.

data.title: The base Keyword
data.text: Use base(...) in a derived class constructor to call the base class constructor. Use base.MethodName() inside an override to call the original base implementation.

An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated directly. It serves as a partial template for derived classes. Abstract classes can contain both abstract members (no implementation, must be overridden) and concrete members (with implementation, optionally overridden). Use abstract classes when you want to share code among related classes while enforcing a common interface.

data.title: Abstract Class with Abstract and Virtual Methods
data.content: A Shape abstract base class with abstract Area() and virtual Display() methods.

data.text: By default, any class can be inherited from. If you want to prevent further inheritance — for security, performance, or design reasons — you can mark a class as `sealed`. A sealed class cannot be used as a base class. You can also seal an individual override with `sealed override` to prevent further derived classes from overriding that specific method.

data.title: Sealed Classes and Sealed Overrides
data.content: Preventing further inheritance and method overriding using sealed.

data.title: Exercise: E-Commerce Class Hierarchy
data.description: Create an abstract Product base class with Name, Price, and an abstract GetDiscountedPrice() method. Create a derived Electronics class that adds WarrantyMonths and overrides GetDiscountedPrice() (10% off if warranty > 12). Create a Clothing class that adds Size and overrides GetDiscountedPrice() (15% off). Test with a List<Product>.
steps: Create abstract class Product with Name, Price, and abstract GetDiscountedPrice().
Create Electronics deriving from Product with WarrantyMonths.
Override GetDiscountedPrice() in Electronics to apply 10% discount if warranty > 12 months.
Create Clothing deriving from Product with Size property.
Override GetDiscountedPrice() in Clothing to apply 15% discount.
Create a List<Product>, add both types, and call GetDiscountedPrice() on each.
data.expectedOutcome: Polymorphic behavior: calling GetDiscountedPrice() on each product returns the correct type-specific discounted price.

items.question: Can a class inherit from multiple classes?
items.answer: No. C# does not support multiple class inheritance (a class can inherit from only one base class). Use interfaces if you need to combine multiple contracts.

items.question: What is the difference between abstract class and interface?
items.answer: Abstract classes can have implemented methods and fields; interfaces (pre-C# 8) can only declare method signatures. Abstract classes support access modifiers on members; interface members are implicitly public. Use abstract classes for shared implementation; use interfaces for flexible contracts.

items.question: What happens if I forget to override an abstract method?
items.answer: The compiler will raise an error. Any non-abstract class that inherits from an abstract class must implement all inherited abstract members.

items.question: Can I inherit from a sealed class?
items.answer: No. Attempting to inherit from a sealed class will result in a compile-time error.

items.question: When should I use inheritance vs composition?
items.answer: Prefer composition ('has-a') over inheritance ('is-a') when the relationship is not a true subtype or when you need flexibility. Inheritance creates tight coupling; composition is more flexible. Ask: 'Does X truly is-a Y?' If uncertain, use composition.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Inheritance creates an 'is-a' relationship between classes.
Derived classes inherit public and protected members from their base class.
Abstract classes cannot be instantiated and enforce method implementation.
sealed prevents a class or override from being further inherited.
data.takeaway: Inheritance enables hierarchical code organization, but use it judiciously — prefer composition when the relationship is not a true subtype.
